clue.text: Welcome in at 6 with meal almost done

indicators.note: something almost done stops just short of the finish, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: tea is an evening meal in Britain

explanation.surface: A host greets guests arriving at six o'clock with dinner nearly ready.
explanation.walkthrough: The 6 looks like a time or a cross-reference, but it is just the Roman numeral; TEA loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To invite someone is to ask them in, extending a welcome, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Gatecrash of fashionable West End reportedly regretted afterwards

indicators.note: says the regret part comes after the other pieces, fixing the order of joining
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept
what is reported is heard, so the word is taken by its sound and then spelt differently

blocks.note: rued means regretted; RUDE sounds the same

explanation.surface: Someone crashes a fashionable party in London's West End and is sorry afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: West End reads as London's theatre district, but it means the end of the word West. The West End is London's theatre and shopping district.
explanation.definitionFit: To gatecrash is to enter uninvited, which is exactly what intruding means; both are verbs.

clue.text: Road without a meeting place

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the single letter named is taken away

explanation.surface: A road with no proper spot to gather.
explanation.definitionFit: A venue is the place where an event or gathering is held, so it is a meeting place.

clue.text: Strife between Belgium and the French after rout at sea

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and disordered, so the letters are jumbled
says the country and article come after the jumbled word, fixing the order

blocks.note: B is the international vehicle code for Belgium

explanation.surface: Discord between Belgium and France after a naval defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'between' looks like a container signal but just links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife means conflict or difficulty, and trouble is a close synonym for that sort of discord.

clue.text: Students turn up in error

indicators.note: turning something up flips it over, so the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: Students arrive by mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip-up is a careless mistake, so it is a noun synonym for error.

clue.text: Drunk on shorts?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone intoxicated by short drinks, spirits served in small measures
setter's reading: shorts are trousers with no legs to speak of, and the slang word for very drunk also means without legs

explanation.walkthrough: Shorts are spirits in British pubs, so being very drunk on them fits; the slang word for very drunk also literally describes legwear lacking legs.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang for helplessly drunk literally means having no legs, which also describes short trousers.

clue.text: Famous seafront hotel holding key model

indicators.note: holding means keeping something inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: prom, short for promenade, is a seafront walkway
an inn is a small hotel

explanation.surface: A well-known hotel on the seafront keeps a key model on display.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes between the two Ns of INN.
explanation.definitionFit: Prominent people are well known and stand out, so the adjective is a synonym for famous.

clue.text: Sharp chap's following play on words

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the man is placed after the wordplay part

blocks.note: a pun is a play on words

explanation.surface: A sharp-witted man comes up with a clever joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Pungent describes a sharp, strong smell or taste, or cutting wit.

clue.text: Wife is typically a bit spirited

indicators.note: a bit means a small part, so the answer is a stretch of the words before it

blocks.note: runs across the end of wife, all of is, and the start of typically

explanation.surface: A sly remark that wives are usually a little lively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'typically' is part of the fodder as well as the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Feisty means lively, determined and full of fight, so it fits spirited.

clue.text: Insist on having stadium seating at United fit for a king to sit in

indicators.note: sitting in something means being placed inside it, so the royal letters go within

blocks.note: a stand is seating at a stadium
GR is Georgius Rex, King George

explanation.surface: A fan demands a stadium seat at Manchester United worthy of royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United' suggests the football club, but it means made one; GR (Georgius Rex) is the royal cipher on British postboxes.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand one's ground is to refuse to give way, which is insisting on one's position.

clue.text: Excellent drink at the Queen's Head bar

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

explanation.surface: A great pint in the bar of a pub called the Queen's Head.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen's Head is a common British pub name, but here it splits: the Queen is ER and Head picks the first letter of bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb means of the highest quality, a direct synonym for excellent.

clue.text: Sample freshly made mince pies I left out

indicators.note: something freshly made is newly put together, so the letters are reworked
left out means omitted, so the named letter is removed from the fodder

explanation.surface: Try one of these freshly baked mince pies, but I did not get one.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop one I from the letters of mince pies, then rearrange the rest. A mince pie is a small British Christmas pastry filled with dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A specimen is a single example taken for testing or display, which is a sample.

clue.text: Salvage from inside of wreck's taking more than a year

indicators.note: the inside of a word is its middle, so the outer letters are dropped

blocks.note: Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: Raising a shipwreck takes over a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvage is the rescuing of goods or a vessel, and recovery is the getting back of what was lost.

clue.text: Rector has problem with musicians

indicators.note: a problem puts things in disarray, so these letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A vicar is having trouble with the church musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' reads as part of the indicator but its letters are fodder too.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large group of instrumental players, so it is a collective of musicians.

clue.text: The French criminal thus framed private eye

indicators.note: criminal means wrong or bent, so the following word's letters are rearranged
a frame goes around a picture, so one piece is placed inside the other

explanation.surface: A French criminal was set up by a detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'framed' plays on criminals being framed, but it means put around.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleuth is a detective, and a private eye is a hired detective.

clue.text: Deals in shares

blocks.note: first meaning: a shop that keeps goods for sale
second meaning: securities traded on a market

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase about a trader, but splits into a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop stocks items it sells, and stocks are also company shares traded on an exchange.

clue.text: Win hands down on old motorbike

blocks.note: second meaning: a classic British motorcycle make

explanation.surface: Someone wins an easy race riding a vintage motorcycle.
explanation.definitionFit: To triumph is to gain a decisive victory, and Triumph is a long-established British motorcycle manufacturer.

clue.text: National coach had up by judge for therapy

indicators.note: in a down entry, brought up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A national team's coach was taken to court and sent for counselling.
explanation.definitionFit: A subject is a citizen owing allegiance to a state, so a national of that country.

clue.text: Comfortably off, having good health and also having old money

indicators.note: having means holding within, so the money letter is put inside

blocks.note: d was the abbreviation for an old British penny

explanation.surface: A description of someone healthy and rich from inherited wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: D, the pre-1971 British penny, sits inside TOO. The first 'having' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-to-do describes people who are prosperous, which is the same as comfortably off.

clue.text: Woman has a horse working heavy cart

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for woman
gee-gee is a childish word for a horse
on means working, as a machine is on

explanation.surface: A woman owns a horse that pulls a heavy cart.
explanation.definitionFit: A waggon (a British spelling of wagon) is a four-wheeled vehicle for heavy loads, so a heavy cart.

clue.text: Romantic Latin lines lifted one with endless serenity

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifted means raised from bottom to top, so read backwards
without its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Latin
RY is short for railway, lines
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Romantic Latin verses lift a person into perfect tranquillity.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyrical writing is expressive and full of feeling, so it is romantic in tone.

clue.text: Lady's maid has drawers

blocks.note: first meaning: a servant who helps someone put on clothes
second meaning: a piece of furniture fitted with drawers

explanation.surface: A lady's maid owns some underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Drawers sounds like old-fashioned knickers; here it means sliding storage boxes, and 'has drawers' describes the item of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A dresser helps someone get clothed, and a dresser is also a cabinet or chest fitted with drawers.

clue.text: Many things combined on road to Times journalist getting the sack

blocks.note: the M1 motorway, written with I for 1

explanation.surface: A Times journalist on the motorway learns they have been fired.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway; 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixed bag is an assortment of varied things, so many different items lumped together.

clue.text: Run out with air gun and point right to thief

blocks.note: RO is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out
a BB gun is an air gun
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A burglar flees, pointing an air gun at someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber is someone who steals, so a thief.

clue.text: Frank James, the singer

blocks.note: second meaning: the surname of the English singer-songwriter James

explanation.surface: Two singers named Frank and James.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank looks like a first name next to James, but it is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Blunt means plain-spoken, a synonym of frank, and James Blunt is the singer of 'You're Beautiful'.

clue.text: Affair on river proceeding as expected?

definitions.note: the phrase names the expected thing; with 'as' before it, it means proceeding as expected

blocks.note: of means on or about, as in 'talk of it'
a course is the channel a river follows

explanation.surface: A romance on a river cruise goes just as everyone predicted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done as a matter of course happens routinely, as would be expected, so the phrase describes the expected outcome.

clue.text: Chap replacing leader of political group is very enthusiastic

indicators.note: replacing the leader means the first letter is taken off and something else goes in its place

blocks.note: he is a man, a chap
a party is a political group

explanation.surface: A man takes over as head of a political party and is full of zeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearty means vigorous and wholehearted, so very enthusiastic.

clue.text: Coat with strange lustre

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so the letters are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A coat that has an odd sheen.
explanation.definitionFit: An ulster is a long, loose overcoat, often belted, named after the Irish province.
